1:
The psalm has no title, and the voices differ over what follows from that. Adam Clarke says the reason is that it was written as part of the psalm before it, as about twenty-seven of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi show; he notes that the Greek and Latin supply a heading of their own, a psalm of David for the sons of Jonadab and the first of those led into captivity. John Calvin reports that by general consent it is ascribed to David and supposed composed during the revolt of Absalom, since he mentions his old age and his danger of perishing; it is almost a copy of an earlier psalm, and because the passages about advanced age are wanting there, it looks as though that psalm, written during the persecution by Saul, was taken and adapted by a little alteration and addition to his later afflictions. Keil and Delitzsch decide otherwise. The psalm begins like one older psalm and closes like another and is throughout an echo of older language, which has become the author’s mental property and is revived in him by similar experiences; and three reasons persuade them it came from the pen of Jeremiah — the age its relationships point to, the anthological weaving of older passages varied by slight touches of his own, which is exactly his manner, and a style slow, loose, sparingly adorned and here and there prosaic.

C.H. Spurgeon distinguishes the two prepositions: we must not only rest on God as a man stands on a rock but trust in him as a man hides in a cave, and though God knows our faith he loves to hear us avow it, which is why the psalmist not only trusts but says so. On the plea against confusion he makes the psalmist’s reputation God’s own concern — if forsaken, men will ridicule his religion and the cause itself be put to shame. Matthew Henry reduces the whole psalm to two petitions, that he might never be confounded and that his persecutors might be, and observes that God will never disappoint a hope of his own raising. Augustine of Hippo takes the psalm for a song of the grace that delivers, and reads it alongside the apostle who called himself the least of the apostles and the chief of sinners — first not in time, he says, but in evil disposition.

The third verse divides on a word. Adam Clarke reports that many of the same manuscripts read not habitation but munition or defence, giving be thou my rock of defence, and takes the clause about a commandment to save as meaning that God has determined the escape and ordered his angels to guard him. Charles Ellicott attends to the other noun, which he would render cliff rather than rock, to distinguish it from the different word used just before. John Gill keeps the habitation and finds it very appropriate, following Kimchi, that David should ask for one when driven out of his dwelling place and palace at Jerusalem by his own son; when God’s people have no certain dwelling place, he adds, they always find one in the Lord, and particularly in his heart’s love, a strong habitation who is called a strong rock, a strong hold and a strong tower, a wall of fire round about them.
4:
John Gill and Adam Clarke both name the wicked man of the fourth verse Absalom, Clarke observing that he is called the Wicked because he violated all laws human and divine, and identifying the unrighteous and cruel man of the same verse with the iniquitous counsellor who advised him. Charles Ellicott attends instead to the title given God in the next verse, my hope, which he traces through the prophets into the New Testament naming of Christ as our hope, and notes that Shakespeare, with his fine ear for scriptural expressions, caught the phrase and used it twice. C.H. Spurgeon makes the hope itself a plea: God who gives the grace to hope will fulfil the hope, and since he cannot be a false or falling hope we may expect to see the confidence justified. On the trust held from youth he counts it a cheering recollection that David had proved his faith by notable exploits when he was young and ruddy.

The sixth verse looks back to birth, and Charles Ellicott finds the received rendering doubtful. The Hebrew word is not the one used in the parallel psalm, and our version translates both alike, treating it as a transitive participle of a verb that elsewhere means only to go through; the Greek has protector, which he thinks an error for a word meaning one who draws out, and that would support the rendering he that severed me, probable for other reasons. He adds that a retrospect from earliest infancy suits Israel personified as an individual as well as the individual himself, and that the psalm has often been treated as an epitome of the history of the Christian Church. C.H. Spurgeon stays with the individual: before he was able to understand the power that preserved him he was sustained by it, for God knows us before we know anything, and the elect lay in the bosom of God before they were laid on their mothers’. John Gill lists the supports — being, life, food and raiment — and notes that the psalmist rehearses them to encourage his own faith for the present deliverance.

In what sense he is a wonder divides the entry sharply. Adam Clarke renders the word as a portent or type and takes it of himself as a typical person, many of the things that happen to him being referred to the one of whom he is a type; alternatively he is a continual prodigy, his low estate, the killing of the lion and the bear, the conquest of the Philistine, the escape from Saul and the raising to the throne being so many wonders of providence. Charles Ellicott turns the word the other way: not a miracle of preservation but a monster, at whom men point as something to be avoided or mocked, though God is his refuge. John Gill agrees that the reference is to the present distress rather than to the preservation or the exploits, since he was obliged to quit his palace and flee from his son with a few servants, and so was a shocking spectacle. John Wesley settles it in six words, that it is for his many and sore calamities. On the mouth filled with praise John Gill offers the alternative rendering, that God’s praise shall fill his mouth, and takes the filling to mean speaking largely and publicly and with great delight.
9:
Whether the ninth verse asks or affirms divides the entry. Adam Clarke says the original might be rendered as a statement rather than a petition — thou wilt not cast me off till the time of old age, and according to the failure of my flesh thou wilt not forsake me — so that the expectation of rest and happiness is not deferred to old age, and as the outward man decays the inward man is renewed day by day. John Gill keeps the petition and answers it with a doctrine: the Lord never casts off those whom he foreknew, but bears and carries them to hoary hairs, so that he who was the guide of David’s youth is asked to be the staff of his age. C.H. Spurgeon puts the fear plainly, that David was not tired of his Master but feared his Master might be tired of him; old age robs a man of beauty and of strength for active service but does not lower him in the love of God, and where an ungrateful country leaves its worn-out defenders on a scanty pittance, the pensioners of heaven are satisfied with good things.

The taunt that God has forsaken him draws the sharpest comment. Adam Clarke reconstructs the reasoning — he who guarded David all his life has now cast him off, so we shall easily prevail; his present adversity shows God is no longer his friend — and then denies the premise outright: this is how men judge, that secular prosperity proves God’s favour and adversity his displeasure, but it is not God’s way, and except in particular judgments he never manifests pleasure or displeasure by outward good or ill. John Gill allows that good men may seem forsaken, and may think themselves so, and may indeed be forsaken for a small moment when God withdraws his gracious presence, but never finally and totally; the enemies inferred it from his distressed condition and said it to one another to encourage themselves to lay hands on him with impunity. C.H. Spurgeon hears dogs howling over a dying lion, and takes the psalmist’s earnestness to be that God’s faithful dealing should give them the lie.

On the closing imprecation Adam Clarke refuses to read a wish at all: they shall be confounded, these being prophetic denunciations rather than curses. Charles Ellicott adds only that the word given as hurt is literally evil. John Gill notes on the intervening plea that God is everywhere present in being, power and providence, so that the distance deprecated is the hiding of his face, which his people cannot bear.
14:
Matthew Henry marks the sudden change of voice at the fourteenth verse: the fears are silenced, the hopes raised, and the prayers turned into thanksgivings — let the enemies say what they will to drive him to despair, he will hope in the most clouded day and hope to the end. C.H. Spurgeon says hope will live on a bare common and sing on a branch laden with snow, and takes the phrase more and more as a refusal to settle down in thankfulness, since we ought to be misers in doing good. John Gill calls hope the anchor of the soul in distress and the helmet that covers the head in the day of battle, exercised most eminently in affliction. Adam Clarke reads it as a bargain of proportion: as the blessings abound, so shall the praises.

On the numbers he cannot reckon Charles Ellicott is exact: mere reminiscence must give place to actual calculation, and that calculation must itself fail before the sense of divine interference in his favour. Adam Clarke draws the practical conclusion, that he must be continually in the spirit of gratitude and obedience because the blessings are innumerable, and that of these alone he will speak. John Wesley supplies the missing noun, the salvations and mercies vouchsafed him. John Gill divides the righteousness to be shown forth into the punitive justice taken on enemies, the faithfulness that performs promises, and the righteousness of Christ accepted and imputed. C.H. Spurgeon makes the duty simpler, that we are to bear testimony as experience enables us and not withhold from others what we have tasted and handled.

The sixteenth verse divides on its verb. Adam Clarke renders it I will enter, meaning into the tabernacle, in the mightinesses of the supreme God who is his prop and stay. Charles Ellicott would have him come rather than go, and come carrying something: I will come with the Lord’s mighty deeds, that is, with the tale of them and the praise of them, into the temple. John Gill canvasses three senses — not in his own strength, since his heart is not always disposed aright for the service; or into the strengths of God, the word being plural to show the greatness of a power that is a garrison and a strong tower to the believer; or into the house of God to perform public worship there.

On being taught from youth John Gill lists what was learned — the corruption of human nature, the insufficiency of his own righteousness, the duties of religion — and ascribes the teaching to God whoever the instruments were, whether his parents or the priests and Levites. Adam Clarke adds that those are well taught whom God instructs, and that when he teaches there is no delay in learning. C.H. Spurgeon turns it into a warning against novelty: a sacred conservatism is much needed when men are giving up old lights for new, and he hopes that grey heads will be found on the same road they trod as beardless youths, unlike those seduced from the school of the gospel into the colleges of philosophy and scepticism. On the final plea Charles Ellicott notes that the words run literally even to old age and grey hairs, that the strength is literally the arm, and that a parallel elsewhere shows the prayer may be national as well as individual. Adam Clarke observes that the grey hairs are added to the old age of the earlier verse because, humanly speaking, they were calculated to make a deeper impression in his favour; and though God needs no such information, he is pleased to invite his children to reason with him, so that in pleading they do precisely what he commanded.
19:
Adam Clarke takes the righteousness reaching to the exalted place as mercy that fills all space, crowning in the heavens what it governed on earth, and turns the question that follows into a doxology on the incomparable and uncompounded Being whose essence is hidden from all created intelligences. Charles Ellicott is occupied with the arrangement of the clauses, which he would set out as three short lines — thy righteousness, O God, to the height; thou who doest great things; God, who is like unto thee? C.H. Spurgeon reads the height as belonging to the plan of righteousness itself, a high-doctrine gospel that gives a high experience and ends in high felicity, and compares the awe of a traveller among the high Alps. John Gill refers the height to the righteousness of Christ, accepted with the Father and infinitely above any righteousness of angel or man.

The twentieth verse is written one way and read another, and both are noticed. Charles Ellicott observes that the written text has quicken us, which he takes as an indication that the psalm is a hymn for congregational use, the change from singular to plural being common enough; and he glosses the depths as abysses, properly of water, perhaps with the waters on which the earth was supposed to rest in view, so that the figure is the familiar sea of trouble. John Gill reports the same divergence between the writing and the marginal reading, noting that the Targum follows the plural, and catalogues the troubles shown to David — the persecution by Saul, the crimes and rebellion in his own family, the curses of Shimei — together with inward ones from the corruptions of his heart and the hidings of God’s face. Adam Clarke keeps the singular and presses one word: God only showed him the troubles, for had he let them fall with their own energy and natural consequences they would have destroyed him. He then applies the quickening to the passion and resurrection, since the Holy One was not to see corruption.

The vow of praise that closes the psalm divides its two most practical readers. Adam Clarke identifies both instruments as stringed and as the principal ones used in Jewish worship, and adds that with these, or anything like them, Christians have nothing to do in divine worship. C.H. Spurgeon takes the opposite line without arguing it, having David give his best music, vocal and instrumental alike, to the best of masters, so that neither his harp nor his voice should be silent. Charles Ellicott reads the next verse as saying that the lips shall sing while the hand plays, so that a hymn should accompany the harp, and denies that any union of bodily and spiritual powers is in view — though he grants the verse naturally suggested that to the Fathers, and allows that the poet’s wish, read across the whole psalm, is that mind and soul according well should make one music, but vaster. C.H. Spurgeon puts the same thought as that soul-singing is the soul of singing. John Gill divides the increased greatness into the temporal, the crushing of the rebellion and the return to his palace, and the spiritual, an enlarged experience and a growing faith; and Adam Clarke ends with the confusion of the enemies as already accomplished in David’s sight, the counsel of the counsellor turned to foolishness and the son meeting the fate he had meditated for his father.
